text.string: Pressure, heat and the machines that make it happen
WHAT EVERY MACHINE IS TRYING TO DO
Hot water, forced at high pressure through finely ground, tightly packed coffee.
18 g of coffee in,36 g espresso out
from pump on tolast drip
Water is drawn from the tank
The pump pushes it up to about 9 bar of pressure
The boiler heats it to about 93 C
Hot, pressurised water is forced through the coffee puck
Espresso pours out, topped with golden crema
Pressure from: your arm or a spring
Pulling the lever lifts a piston and lets water in.A spring (or your arm) then pushes it down, sopressure starts near 9 bar and gently falls off.
Found in: classic cafe levers and manual home machines
PULL DOWN, LET THE SPRING PUSH
An electromagnet snaps a small piston back andforth 50-60 times a second, pushing waterthrough in rapid pulses.
Found in: most home espresso machines
A motor spins a disc with sliding vanes inside anoff-centre chamber, sweeping water through forsmooth, constant pressure.
Can be plumbed into mains water
Found in: cafe machines and high-end home setups
One button grinds the beans, doses, tamps,brews the shot and dumps the used puck- all inside the machine.
Found in: offices and busy homes
Pressure from: a small vibratory pump
A sealed capsule of pre-ground coffee is piercedand hot water is pumped straight through it.No grinding, no tamping.
Found in: kitchens that want coffee in seconds
